newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Daimler trims fat in efficiency drive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Daimler trims fat in efficiency drive.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG approved a sweeping restructuring plan on Thursday which ends the existence of Mercedes-Benz as a separate unit --aimed at cutting costs and boosting the industrial giant's international competitiveness.

Daimler said that its supervisory board approved plans that will merge Mercedes-Benz, the backbone of Daimler's business, into the group structure. It leaves the group's two other main units, Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) and Debis AG, as fully separate legal entities.

"The new structure is a milestone in the drive to increase the company's earnings potential and will provide a flexible framework for the further evolution of our business portfolio," Daimler chairman Juergen Schrempp said in a statement.
As part of the restructuring, the Mercedes division will be represented by three executives on Daimler's management board, increasing the board's overall size to 10 from seven.

The industrial giant first published details of the reorganisation last Thursday, announcing most significantly that Mercedes-Benz boss Helmut Werner had resigned because he saw no room for himself in the overhauled group structure.
Daimler did not say how much money the reorganisation, which takes effect from April1, would save. But it said the new structure could cut central administrative costs by 30 percent.
The supervisory board is a group of leading independent executives from outside the Daimler group who have an advisory role similar to the board of directors at U.S. companies.
Although DASA and financial services and information technology company Debis will remain independent, the size of their head offices will be reduced.
At DASA, the separate management structures for Aircraft, Space Systems and Defence units will be eliminated.
The three executives joining the Daimler management board had been members of Mercedes-Benz's management board and will represent the same business areas that they had in the past.
Juergen Hubbert will be in charge of passenger cars, Kurt Lauk will head commercial vehicle operations and Dieter Zetsche is to take over a board position for sales and marketing.
Daimler, which has been working on the restructuring for about a year, had long been considered top-heavy with management, slowing decision-making and reducing accountability.

Schrempp, who took over Daimler in 1995, has led a virtual crusade to cut costs, slashing unprofitable units such as Deutsch Aircraft maker Fokker NV, and laying down strict profit goals for Daimler's 23 operating units.

Daimler sources said the plan that was finalised on Thursday, ending a financial holding structure first put into place in 1989, was born of the realisation that Mercedes will remain the bulk of the group's business well into the next century.

"As a result of the restructuring, the divisional managers will have a significantly larger measure of responsibility, and will be able to function as true entrepreneurs," Schrempp said in the statement.

The financial community, although disappointed at the loss of Werner, has applauded Daimler's restructuring plan as continued evidence of Schrempp's commitment to making the company, Germany's largest, more profitable.

Although the overhaul will intially drive up costs as middle and upper level managers are moved elsewhere in the company or leave it all together, analysts said the package could result in savings of several hundred million marks a year.
